title: The Time Is Fulfilled
sum: Mark opens without a birth story. Scripture promised a messenger and a voice in the wilderness, and John appears at the Jordan, dressed like Elijah, calling Israel to a baptism of repentance and pointing to a stronger one who will baptize in the Holy Spirit. Jesus comes from Nazareth, is baptized, sees the heavens torn open and the Spirit come down, and hears God's voice: "You are my dearly loved Son." At once the Spirit throws him into the wilderness, where Satan tests him among wild animals and angels serve him.

Then the action races forward. Jesus announces that God's kingdom has drawn near, calls four fishermen, teaches with authority in the Capernaum synagogue, throws out an unclean spirit, raises Simon's mother-in-law from her fever and heals a whole town at sunset. Before dawn he prays alone, then moves on to preach in other towns. A man with a skin disease begs to be made clean; Jesus touches him, heals him and sends him to the priest, but the man spreads the news, and Jesus can no longer enter towns openly.
readings: Read as a day in the life

Mark 1:21–34 tells one Sabbath in Capernaum, from synagogue to sunset, and 1:35 the next dawn. Many scholars think this "day" was shaped as a sample of Jesus' work: teaching, exorcism, healing, prayer and moving on. The tradition that Mark drew on Peter's memories (see the book introduction) would explain why the day centers on Peter's town and house.
Read as the opening of a cosmic battle

The chapter is full of powers: the Spirit who comes into Jesus and drives him out, Satan who tests him, unclean spirits who shriek and obey. The heavens are split open, and the one stronger than John begins to take back what the strong man holds (3:27). Read this way, the healings are not only kindnesses but signs that God's rule is breaking into a world held captive.

views.H: Jesus' baptism by John is one of the best-attested facts about him, and Josephus confirms John's movement and its popularity. Capernaum, a lakeside town on the border between the lands of Herod Antipas and Philip, fits a teacher who drew crowds from many directions. Exorcisms and healings are reported of Jesus by friends and enemies alike (3:22); historians of every background, such as John Meier and E. P. Sanders, accept that he was known as a healer and exorcist, whatever they make of the cause.
views.C: Most scholars think Mark was written first and that Matthew and Luke used it. Chapter 1 supplies classic evidence: Matthew and Luke add birth stories before it, expand the testing from two verses into three scenes, and drop or soften Mark's rougher details: the Spirit "throwing" Jesus out (1:12), Jesus' anger or snorting at the healed man (1:41, 43), the wild animals (1:13). Those who hold the minority Griesbach view (Mark used Matthew and Luke) explain the same data as Mark's abridging and sharpening. The composite quotation in 1:2–3 and the variant "in the prophets" show that early scribes noticed difficulties in Mark's text.
views.L: Mark moves fast: "right away" appears eleven times in this chapter. The prologue (1:1–13 or 1:1–15) tells the reader what the characters do not know: Jesus is God's Son, filled with the Spirit, the Lord whose road was prepared. From then on the reader watches people try to work out who he is. The torn heavens (1:10) will be matched by the torn curtain (15:38). The commands to silence (1:25, 34, 44) begin the "messianic secret."
views.J: Everything here takes place inside Jewish life: a prophet in the line of Elijah, purity washings, the Sabbath synagogue, the Law's procedure for skin disease. Jesus sends the cleansed man to the priest "as Moses ordered" (1:44) and waits with the town for the Sabbath to end (1:32). Jewish scholars such as Geza Vermes compare Jesus to Galilean holy men like Hanina ben Dosa, famous for healing and prayer. The "unclean spirit" uses purity language: Jesus' holiness overcomes impurity rather than being stained by it.
views.T: The Eastern churches celebrate Jesus' baptism on January 6 as Theophany, the revealing of the Trinity. In the West, Mark was long read as a shorter Matthew (Augustine called Mark Matthew's "follower and abbreviator"), and its opening was little preached. Jerome linked Mark with the lion among the four living creatures of Ezekiel 1 and Revelation 4 because his Gospel opens with a voice roaring in the wilderness; hence the lion of Saint Mark in Venice, whose church claimed his relics from 828.

deep.b:
Each Gospel begins in its own way: Matthew with Abraham and David, Luke with the Temple in Jerusalem, John before creation. Mark begins at the Jordan, with an adult Jesus, and in fifteen verses brings together the whole background: Scripture (1:2–3), the forerunner (1:4–8), the baptism and the voice (1:9–11), the testing (1:12–13) and the first announcement (1:14–15). Some scholars end the prologue at 1:13, others at 1:15; the word "good news" in 1:1 and 1:14–15 frames it either way.

The prologue lets the reader in on the secret. We hear the voice from heaven; the crowd at the river does not. We know Jesus is "the Lord" of Isaiah 40:3. That knowledge makes the rest of the Gospel full of irony: demons recognize Jesus (1:24, 34), religious experts call him a blasphemer (2:7), his family think him mad (3:21), and his disciples keep misunderstanding him. The reader is asked to keep watching what kind of Son and Messiah this is, until the centurion at the cross (15:39).

deep.h: "Jesus' heart went out" or "Jesus grew angry"? (1:41)
deep.b:
At 1:41 the SBLGNT, followed here, prints orgistheis, "having become angry," with Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies, against nearly every other manuscript, which read splanchnistheis, "moved with compassion." The case for "angry" rests on the principle that the harder reading is more likely original: scribes would soften anger into compassion, not the reverse. It is supported by Matthew's and Luke's silence about Jesus' feelings here, though both keep compassion elsewhere, and by the harsh words of 1:43. The case for "compassion" rests on the overwhelming spread of manuscripts, early and late, east and west.

The choice matters for how readers picture Jesus, but not for what he does: in either reading he chooses the man ("I want to"), touches him, cleans him and sends him back into the life of Israel. Mark's Jesus feels anger again at hard hearts (3:5) and is indignant with his own disciples (10:14). See the variant for the witnesses and the scholars on each side.

echoes: Isaiah 40:3; Malachi 3:1; Exodus 23:20; 2 Kings 1:8; Isaiah 64:1; Psalm 2:7; Genesis 22:2; Isaiah 42:1; Exodus 34:28; 1 Kings 19:5–8; 1 Kings 19:19–21; Jeremiah 16:16; Leviticus 13:45–46; Leviticus 14:1–32; Matthew 3:1–4:25; Matthew 8:1–4; Matthew 8:14–17; Luke 3:1–22; Luke 4:1–44; Luke 5:12–16; John 1:19–42

settings.what: The opening quotation of Scripture
settings.to: The Gospel's readers
settings.when: Before the story begins
settings.why: To set Jesus' story inside Israel's Scriptures from the first line. By joining Exodus 23:20, Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3, Mark tells readers that God's long-promised return to his people is happening, that John is the messenger, and that the "Lord" whose road is prepared is Jesus.
settings.readers: For a persecuted church, possibly in Rome, the quotation said that their faith was no new cult but the fulfillment of Israel's oldest hopes.

settings.what: John's preaching about the one to come
settings.to: The crowds from Judea and Jerusalem who came out to the Jordan to be baptized
settings.when: During John's baptizing in the wilderness, before Jesus appears
settings.why: To turn attention from himself to one far greater, whose baptism with the Holy Spirit would fulfill what John's water only pointed to. For hearers who saw John as a prophet, perhaps even as the hoped-for deliverer, the words set him in his place: a servant unfit to untie the coming one's sandals. Matthew aims John's preaching at the Pharisees and Sadducees who came for baptism (Matthew 3:7), and Luke at the crowds (Luke 3:7); Mark names no target beyond the people streaming out from Judea and Jerusalem.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, who had been baptized and received the Spirit, would hear John's promise as fulfilled in their own experience; any who still honored John above Jesus (compare Acts 19:1–7) are corrected.

settings.what: The voice from heaven
settings.by: God, speaking from the torn heavens
settings.to: Jesus himself ("You are"); in Mark only Jesus is said to see the vision
settings.when: As Jesus comes up out of the Jordan after John baptizes him
settings.why: To declare and confirm Jesus' identity and calling at the start of his work: the royal Son of Psalm 2, the beloved son like Isaac, the servant on whom God's Spirit rests (Isaiah 42:1). Because the words are spoken to Jesus, they are a personal commission, not a public proclamation.
settings.readers: The reader overhears what the crowd does not, and so watches the rest of the story knowing what the characters must discover.

settings.what: Jesus' first proclamation
settings.to: The people of Galilee, in towns and villages
settings.when: After John is arrested, at the start of Jesus' public work
settings.why: To announce that God's appointed time has come and his rule is breaking in, and to call every hearer to turn their lives around and trust this news. The arrest of John shows the cost; Jesus begins exactly where John was silenced.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, who call their message "the good news," are shown its source in Jesus' own words and are called to the same repentance and faith.

settings.what: The call of the first disciples
settings.to: Simon and Andrew at their nets; then James and John in their father's boat (1:20)
settings.when: On the shore of the Sea of Galilee, soon after Jesus begins preaching
settings.why: To summon working men to leave their trade and family business and follow him, and to give their skill a new purpose: gathering people for God's kingdom. The call is brief and the response immediate, showing the authority of Jesus' word.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, many of whom had left homes and families (10:28–30), would see their own costly following in these first four.

settings.what: Teaching and an exorcism in the synagogue
settings.by: Jesus; the unclean spirit speaking through the man
settings.to: The Sabbath congregation in the Capernaum synagogue
settings.when: On the first Sabbath of Jesus' work in Capernaum
settings.why: Mark does not record the teaching; he records its effect. The spirit's cry tries to master Jesus by naming him; Jesus silences it with a word and frees the man. The congregation is meant to see that Jesus' teaching and his power are one: his authority is new and direct, not borrowed from tradition.
settings.readers: For readers living among rival cults and magic, the scene shows that Jesus needs no spells: his word is enough.

settings.what: Jesus prays alone
settings.to: God
settings.when: Before dawn, after the crowded evening of healing
settings.why: Mark gives no words of the prayer. Its setting says enough: after his first success, Jesus withdraws to seek his Father, and comes back resolved to move on rather than stay where he is popular.
settings.readers: Mark's readers learn that Jesus' power is rooted in prayer, and that popularity is not the measure of his mission.

settings.what: "Let's head elsewhere"
settings.to: Simon and the others who came hunting for him
settings.when: At dawn, in a deserted place outside Capernaum
settings.why: To resist the disciples' wish to keep him where the crowds were waiting, and to make clear that his calling is to preach the kingdom in every town, not to be a local healer.
settings.readers: For a church spreading the good news beyond its first home, the saying gives Jesus' own example of moving on.

settings.what: Instructions to the cleansed man (the law of cleansing)
settings.to: The man healed of skin disease
settings.when: Right after the cleansing, as Jesus sends him away
settings.why: To send him through the Law's procedure (Leviticus 14): a priest's inspection and the offerings Moses commanded, which bound every Israelite healed of skin disease and were performed at the Temple. That would restore him to his family and community and serve as evidence of the healing. The order to say nothing protects Jesus' mission from turning into a show of wonders.
settings.readers: Mark's mostly Gentile readers learn that Jesus honored the Law's provisions for purity, and the man's disobedience shows how impossible it was to keep Jesus' power hidden.

traditions.q: At the baptism the Father speaks, the Son stands in the water and the Spirit comes down (1:10–11). Does this show one God in three persons?
views: Yes. The feast of Theophany (January 6) celebrates the baptism as the first clear revealing of the Holy Trinity: "the worship of the Trinity was made manifest," as its hymn sings. The Father bears witness, the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends, three persons, one God.

Yes. The baptism is a manifestation of the Trinity and of Jesus as the beloved Son and servant who takes on himself the sins of the world; the Spirit's coming marks him as the Messiah (Catechism 535–536).

Yes. The Westminster Confession teaches one God in three persons of one substance, Father, Son and Holy Spirit (2.3), and Reformed teachers from Calvin on point to the baptism as a scene where the three are distinct at once.

No. God is one person who reveals himself as Father, in the Son (the man Christ Jesus) and as the Holy Spirit. At the Jordan the one God spoke from heaven and anointed the man Jesus with his Spirit; the scene shows God's manifestations, not three persons.

No. The voice is Jehovah's, the only true God; Jesus is his Son, a distinct and lesser being; and the holy spirit is God's active force, not a person. At his baptism Jesus was anointed with holy spirit to be the Christ.

title: Who Can Forgive Sins?
sum: Back in Capernaum, a crowd fills the house where Jesus is speaking. Four men dig through the roof and lower a paralyzed friend. Jesus tells him his sins are forgiven; scribes think this is blasphemy, since only the one God forgives. Jesus answers by healing the man, so they may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. He then calls Levi from his toll booth and eats with tax collectors and sinners, and when scribes of the Pharisees object, he says the sick are the ones who need a doctor.

Questions keep coming. Why do his disciples not fast? Because the groom is with them; when he is taken away, they will fast. New cloth and new wine need new containers. When his disciples pull off heads of grain on the Sabbath, Jesus recalls David eating the Presence Bread and declares that the Sabbath came into being for human beings, and that the Son of Man is Lord even over the Sabbath.
readings: Mark 2:1–3:6 gathers five debates: forgiveness, eating with sinners, fasting, grain on the Sabbath, healing on the Sabbath. Joanna Dewey showed that they form a ring: the first and last are healings in which Jesus reads hostile hearts; the second and fourth are about eating; the fasting question stands in the middle, with its hint that the groom will be "taken away." The ring ends with a plot to kill him (3:6).

Every question here was a live issue among Jews: who may declare forgiveness, how to treat the wicked, when to fast, what the Sabbath allows. Jewish scholars note that Jesus argues from Scripture like a teacher of Israel (David, the creation of the Sabbath) and that some of his answers have close rabbinic parallels (2:27). The debates are sharp, but they are family arguments over the meaning of the Torah, not attacks on it.

views.H: Capernaum's toll booth, the flat roofs of village houses and Pharisaic table fellowship fit first-century Galilee. Historians widely accept that Jesus ate with people regarded as sinners and that this drew criticism, since it is reported in several independent sources (Matthew 11:19; Luke 15:1–2). Whether Pharisees policed fields on the Sabbath in Galilee is doubted by some (E. P. Sanders), who think the story reflects later debates in the church.
views.C: Luke keeps all five in Mark's order (Luke 5:17–6:11). Matthew keeps the first three together (Matthew 9:1–17) and the two Sabbath stories together, later (Matthew 12:1–14). Most scholars count such agreements in order as evidence that Matthew and Luke used Mark, though supporters of the Griesbach view read the same data the other way. They also smooth details: Luke changes the dug-through roof to "tiles" (Luke 5:19); both omit the name of Abiathar (2:26) and the saying that the Sabbath came into being for human beings (2:27). Form critics such as Rudolf Bultmann classed these as "controversy dialogues" shaped by the early church's own disputes, for example over whether Christians should fast (2:20).
views.L: Mark builds suspense. The scribes only think their objections (2:6); the Pharisees ask his disciples (2:16); people ask Jesus about fasting (2:18); the Pharisees challenge him directly (2:24); and in 3:6 they plot his death. The title "Son of Man" frames the chapter (2:10, 28). "The groom will be taken away" (2:20) is the first shadow of the cross.
views.J: The scribes defend a core Jewish belief, that only the one God forgives sins (2:7, echoing the Shema), and Mark does not mock it. The Pharisees' concern for purity at meals and for keeping the Sabbath is a concern for holiness. The saying of 2:27 has a close parallel in the Mekhilta, and saving life was agreed to override the Sabbath. Daniel Boyarin reads the Son of Man sayings here as a Jewish claim to divine authority drawn from Daniel 7, made inside Judaism, not against it.
views.T: The healing of the paralyzed man has long been read as a picture of the church's ministry of forgiveness: the Catholic and Orthodox churches see in 2:10 the root of the authority to absolve sins that Christ gives his apostles (John 20:23; see the card at Matthew 9). The parallel call of Matthew (Matthew 9:9–13) is read on his feast. The Lord of the Sabbath sayings shaped debates over Sunday and the Sabbath: the general question is the card at Matthew 12; the card here asks only what 2:27's "for human beings" adds.

deep.b:
Mark sets five stories side by side, and many scholars, following Joanna Dewey, see a careful pattern:

A. Healing of a paralyzed man: authority to forgive, hidden thoughts read (2:1–12)
B. Eating with tax collectors and sinners (2:13–17)
C. Fasting, and the groom taken away (2:18–22)
B'. Eating grain on the Sabbath (2:23–28)
A'. Healing a withered hand: hard hearts, a plot (3:1–6)

The center holds the first hint of Jesus' death. The opposition grows from silent thoughts to open plotting, and the debates end with Pharisees and Herodians agreeing to destroy him. In chapter 12 Mark gives a similar series in Jerusalem (12:13–37), so the Galilean debates and the Jerusalem debates frame the ministry.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the tear in the coat and the tear in the heavens
deep.b: Mark uses the verb schizō, "split, tear," twice: of the heavens at the baptism (1:10) and of the Temple curtain at Jesus' death (15:38). Readers have long seen those two as a frame. I suggest a third, smaller link in the middle: in 2:21 the patch of new cloth pulls away from the old and "the tear [schisma] gets worse." The saying sits at the exact center of Mark's ring of five debates (see above), next to the first hint of Jesus' death (2:20). If Mark heard his own word, the patch saying may hint that the coming of the new will cause a tearing, which the reader later sees in the torn curtain. Commentators note the word but, as far as I know, do not usually connect it with 1:10 and 15:38; this connection is my own suggestion and is speculative. It does not imply that Judaism is the "old coat" to be discarded; the tearing in Mark is God's opening of access, from heaven and in the sanctuary.

echoes: Psalm 103:3; Deuteronomy 6:4; Daniel 7:13–14; Leviticus 24:16; Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20; Isaiah 53:8; Deuteronomy 23:25; Exodus 34:21; 1 Samuel 21:1–6; Leviticus 24:5–9; Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 31:13–14; Matthew 9:1–17; Matthew 12:1–8; Luke 5:17–39; Luke 6:1–5

settings.what: Forgiveness and the Son of Man
settings.to: The paralyzed man, and the scribes sitting in the crowded house
settings.when: In Capernaum, after four friends lower the man through the roof
settings.why: To meet the man's deepest need first, then to answer the scribes' unspoken charge of blasphemy by a visible sign: the healing proves that the Son of Man has God's authority to forgive sins on earth. The scribes are meant to see that Jesus' claim is backed by God's power.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, who received forgiveness in Jesus' name, are shown its basis in his own authority; the charge of blasphemy also prepares them for his trial (14:64).

settings.what: The call of Levi
settings.to: Levi son of Alphaeus, at his toll booth
settings.when: Beside the lake, as Jesus passes
settings.why: To call a despised tax agent with the same two words he used for the fishermen, showing that following Jesus is open to people the pious kept at a distance.
settings.readers: For a church of mixed and often low-status members, the call shows that no trade or reputation shuts anyone out.

settings.what: "Sick people need a doctor"
settings.to: The scribes of the Pharisees who questioned his disciples
settings.when: At a meal with many tax collectors and sinners
settings.why: To defend his table fellowship with the openly wicked by a proverb: a healer goes to the sick. It turns their objection into a description of his mission: to call sinners. In Matthew 9:11 the questioners are simply the Pharisees, and in Luke 5:30 the Pharisees and their scribes; only Mark calls them the scribes who belonged to the Pharisees.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, who shared meals across lines of class and nation, learn that Jesus' table set the pattern.

settings.what: The groom and the wedding guests
settings.to: People who asked why his disciples did not fast like John's disciples and the Pharisees' disciples
settings.when: On an occasion when those groups were fasting
settings.why: To explain that his presence is a wedding time, when fasting would be out of place, and to hint that a time of grief is coming when the groom will be taken away. In Matthew 9:14 John's disciples ask, about their own fasting; in Luke 5:33 the question comes from the Pharisees and scribes of the meal before. Mark leaves the questioners unnamed.
settings.readers: Mark's church, which fasted, is given the reason: they fast because the groom was taken away, and they await his return.
views: The saying explains why Jesus' disciples did not keep the voluntary fasts of other pious groups.
Some critics think 2:20 was added or shaped to justify the church's later return to fasting, on Fridays in memory of Jesus' death (compare Didache 8:1).

settings.what: Parables of the patch and the wineskins
settings.to: The same questioners about fasting
settings.when: Continuing his answer about fasting
settings.why: To show by two everyday images that what Jesus brings cannot simply be stitched onto existing forms of piety; it needs fitting containers. The point concerns the new time of the groom's presence, not a rejection of Israel's faith.
settings.readers: Readers in a young movement working out its practices are told that new wine needs fresh skins; Luke's added line (Luke 5:39) keeps respect for the old.

settings.what: David, the Presence Bread and the Lord of the Sabbath (Sabbath law)
settings.to: Pharisees who objected to his disciples' picking grain on the Sabbath
settings.when: On a Sabbath, walking through grain fields in Galilee
settings.why: The question was how the Sabbath law of the Torah (Exodus 20:8–11; 34:21), which bound every Israelite household, applied to picking grain; the Pharisees counted it as forbidden harvesting. Jesus answers from Scripture: David's need outweighed a sacred rule, the Sabbath was made for human good, and the Son of Man has authority over it. The answer claims for Jesus the right to say what the Sabbath is for.
settings.readers: Mark's largely Gentile church, which did not keep Jewish Sabbath law, would hear that Jesus himself is Lord of the day; Jewish-Christian readers would hear an argument within the Law, not against it.

traditions.q: "The Sabbath came into being for the sake of human beings" (2:27). Does that make the seventh-day Sabbath a gift and law for all humanity from creation, Gentiles included? (For whether Christians must keep the Sabbath at all, see the card at Matthew 12.)
views: Yes. The Sabbath was made at creation (Genesis 2:2–3) for all humankind, before Israel existed, so Jesus' words show it is binding on every person; the seventh day, Saturday, remains God's holy day, and Jesus kept it as its Lord.

Seventh Day Baptists, a small Baptist body older than Adventism, answer yes: the seventh day is "a gift of God to all people," instituted at creation and reaffirmed by Jesus, and 2:27 is a key text for them. Most Baptists keep Sunday as the Lord's Day instead (see Matthew 12).

The principle of one day in seven is a moral law from creation, binding on all people, but the day was changed at the resurrection to the first day, "the Christian Sabbath," to be kept holy in rest and worship (Westminster Confession 21.7–8).

The Sabbath, the seventh day, is fulfilled in Sunday, the day of Christ's resurrection and the "first day" of the new creation. Christians keep the Lord's Day by worship and rest, and Jesus' words show that the day serves human good and works of mercy (Catechism 2172–2176, 2185).

No. The Sabbath was a sign of the covenant between God and Israel (Exodus 31:13–17), not given to the church; Christians meet on the Lord's Day by choice, and 2:27 teaches the Sabbath's purpose for those under it, not its extension to Gentiles.

title: Who Are My Mother and My Brothers?
sum: On another Sabbath, in a synagogue, people watch to see if Jesus will heal a man with a withered hand. He asks whether it is right on the Sabbath to save a life or to kill, looks at them with anger and grief at their hard hearts, and heals the man. The Pharisees go out and plot with the Herodians to destroy him. Crowds pour in from every region, unclean spirits fall before him crying that he is the Son of God, and he orders them to keep silent.

On a mountain Jesus forms the Twelve, to be with him and to be sent out, and names Simon "Peter." Back home, crowds press in so that no one can eat. His own people set out to seize him, saying he is out of his mind, while scribes from Jerusalem say he works by Beelzebul. Jesus answers in parables: a divided kingdom cannot last, and no one can rob a strong man's house without tying him up. Then his mother and brothers arrive and stand outside. Looking at those seated around him, he says that whoever does God's will is his brother, sister and mother.
readings: Read as the forming of a new Israel

Twelve men chosen on a mountain, like the twelve tribes formed at Sinai; a new family of those who do God's will. Read this way, chapter 3 shows Jesus gathering a renewed people of God around himself, while the authorities who should have recognized him oppose him.
Read as a story of misunderstanding

Almost everyone in the chapter misreads Jesus: the synagogue watchers, the Pharisees and Herodians, the scribes from Jerusalem, even his own family. Only the unclean spirits name him rightly, and he silences them. The chapter asks the reader where they stand: outside, sending messages, or inside, sitting around him.

views.H: Herod Antipas' supporters had reason to watch any popular movement in Galilee after John's arrest. Crowds from Idumea, Perea, Tyre and Sidon show how far news traveled along trade routes. The choice of twelve followers is widely accepted as historical; Paul already knows "the Twelve" (1 Corinthians 15:5). The charge that Jesus worked by Beelzebul, which the Gospels would hardly invent, is good evidence that even opponents granted his exorcisms.
views.C: Matthew and Luke both omit Jesus' anger and grief (3:5), the family's attempt to seize him (3:21), and the comment of 3:30. Matthew and Luke share a longer form of the Beelzebul debate (Matthew 12:22–30; Luke 11:14–23), including a saying about the "finger" or "Spirit of God," which Mark lacks: a classic overlap of Mark and the sayings source Q. The lists of the Twelve vary in one name (Thaddaeus or Judas son of James).
views.L: Chapter 3 contains Mark's first "sandwich": family (3:20–21), scribes (3:22–30), family again (3:31–35). Space carries meaning: the family stands outside, the new family sits in a circle around Jesus, preparing for "those outside" in 4:11. The word "strong" links John's promise (1:7) to the strong man of 3:27. Judas is introduced as "the one who also handed him over," so the shadow of betrayal falls on the Twelve from their first naming.
views.J: The Sabbath healing turns on a principle Jews shared, that saving life overrides the Sabbath (Mishnah Yoma 8:6), and on how far that principle reaches. The Twelve evoke the hope for the regathering of Israel's tribes. Jewish readers note that the Beelzebul charge reflects real fears about sorcery, and that the later Jewish polemic against Jesus as a magician (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 43a) grew from the same memory. The scribes come from Jerusalem, a sign that Mark sets the leaders, not the Jewish people, against Jesus.
views.T: The naming of Peter and the order of the Twelve feed later discussion of Peter's place among the apostles. The saying on the unforgivable sin has been read in the church as a warning against hardened, final refusal of God's grace. The words of 3:31–35 were long read alongside the question of Jesus' brothers and Mary's virginity: Catholic and Orthodox teachers stress that Mary, who did God's will above all, is honored by this saying, not set aside.

deep.b:
Mark often begins a story, interrupts it with another, and then finishes the first. Scholars call these "intercalations" or "sandwiches." James Edwards counts about nine, among them 3:20–35 (family and scribes), 5:21–43 (Jairus' daughter and the bleeding woman), 6:7–30 (the mission of the Twelve and John's death), 11:12–25 (the fig tree and the Temple), 14:1–11 (the plot and the anointing) and 14:54–72 (Peter's denial and Jesus' trial). The two stories interpret each other.

In 3:20–35 the family's verdict, "He is beside himself," sits beside the scribes' verdict, "He has an unclean spirit." Both misread him. Jesus' warning about blasphemy against the Spirit falls between them, and the closing scene redefines family. Readers have debated whether Mark means to put the family on the same level as the scribes; most think he shows misunderstanding by those closest to Jesus, which also prepares for the disciples' failures later.

echoes: 1 Kings 13:4–6; Mishnah Yoma 8:6; Exodus 19:20; Exodus 24:4; Ezekiel 37:15–28; Numbers 25:11; Joshua 15:25; 2 Kings 1:2; Isaiah 49:24–25; Psalm 69:8; Exodus 20:12; Matthew 12:9–32; Matthew 12:46–50; Matthew 10:1–4; Luke 6:6–19; Luke 11:14–23; Luke 8:19–21; John 7:3–5

settings.what: Healing on the Sabbath (Sabbath law)
settings.to: The man with the withered hand, and the people in the synagogue watching for a reason to accuse him
settings.when: On a Sabbath, in a Galilean synagogue
settings.why: The question was whether the Torah's Sabbath rest, binding on every Israelite, allowed healing a condition that was not life-threatening; all agreed that danger to life overrode the Sabbath. Jesus widens the principle: on God's day, withholding good is a kind of harm. He heals by a word, so that no work is done, and exposes the hardness of those who would rather accuse than see a man restored.
settings.readers: Mark's readers learn why Jesus' enemies wanted him dead, and that Jesus' Sabbath practice was a matter of doing good, not of disregarding God's day.

settings.what: The spirits' cry and Jesus' order to silence
settings.to: Jesus; the spirits
settings.when: By the lake, among the crowds that pressed on him for healing
settings.why: The spirits proclaim Jesus' true identity, perhaps to master him or expose him. Jesus refuses their testimony: he will not be made known by demons, nor as a mere wonder-worker, before his identity can be understood through the cross.
settings.readers: Readers hear the truth of 1:1 and 1:11 confirmed even by the enemy, and are taught to receive it from Jesus' own way of the cross, not from displays of power.

settings.what: The appointment of the Twelve
settings.to: The twelve men he summoned on the mountain
settings.when: After the first wave of conflict and crowds
settings.why: To form a core group whose first task was to be with him, and then to be sent out to preach and to throw out demons with his authority. The number twelve signals the renewal of Israel's twelve tribes. The new names given to Simon, James and John mark a new identity.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, who looked to the apostles as founders, are reminded that the Twelve were chosen by Jesus' will, not their own merit, and that even one of them handed him over.

settings.what: Parables of the divided kingdom and the strong man
settings.to: The scribes who had come down from Jerusalem and said he worked by Beelzebul
settings.when: In or near the house in Capernaum, while the crowd pressed in
settings.why: To show that their charge is absurd, since Satan would not destroy his own kingdom, and to explain what is really happening: someone stronger has come, has bound the strong man and is freeing his captives. Matthew 12:22–24 sets the charge after Jesus heals a blind and mute man and gives it to the Pharisees; Luke 11:14–15 gives it to some of the crowd after a mute man is healed. Only Mark has scribes come down from Jerusalem, and only Mark frames the dispute with Jesus' family (3:21, 31–35).
settings.readers: Readers facing a world of hostile powers are told that Satan's rule has been broken by Jesus.

settings.what: The warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit
settings.to: The same scribes from Jerusalem
settings.when: Concluding his answer to their charge
settings.why: To promise forgiveness for every sin and blasphemy, and to warn that calling the Holy Spirit's work of freeing people an unclean spirit puts a person beyond forgiveness. Mark's comment (3:30) ties the warning to this specific charge.
settings.readers: Readers anxious that they might have committed this sin are shown its context: a deliberate refusal to see God at work in Jesus, not a stray word.

settings.what: "Who is my mother?"
settings.to: The crowd sitting around him, with his mother and brothers standing outside
settings.when: When his family arrive and send for him
settings.why: To declare that the people gathered to hear him and do God's will are his true family, a family open to brothers, sisters and mothers. It does not reject his relatives but sets doing God's will above ties of blood. In Matthew 12:49 Jesus points to his disciples; Mark has him look around at the people sitting in a circle around him, a wider group than the Twelve. Luke 8:19–21 sets the saying after the parables, not after the Beelzebul dispute.
settings.readers: For believers who had lost family because of their faith, the saying promised a new family in the church (10:29–30).
